title: Episode 179: John F. Kennedy: PT-109, the Coconut Shell, and the New Frontier (1943–1960)

Before he was the charismatic thirty-fifth President of the United States, John Fitzgerald Kennedy was a sickly, bookish young naval lieutenant stationed in the war-torn Solomon Islands. In the pitch-black early hours of August 2, 1943, the Japanese destroyer Amagiri sliced his wooden patrol torpedo boat, PT-109, cleanly in two, killing two crewmen instantly and leaving eleven survivors clinging to a flaming hull. Showing breathtaking physical endurance despite a chronic spinal injury, Kennedy clamped the strap of a badly burned sailor's life vest between his teeth and towed him for four grueling hours across three miles of shark-infested open ocean to a tiny desert island. Carving an emergency rescue message into the husk of a green coconut, Kennedy entrusted it to two brave Melanesian island scouts, orchestrating an improbable rescue that made him a national hero. Discover the youth, wit, and dazzling ascent of Jack Kennedy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the captivating, charismatic world of John Fitzgerald Kennedy. With JFK, American politics entered a dazzling new era of television, cultural glamour, quick wit, and youthful vigor. But long before the White House, Kennedy faced death in the dark waters of the Pacific. Here is George with the story of PT-109, the coconut shell, and the dawn of the New Frontier.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE GOLDEN CLAN OF HYANNIS PORT
John Fitzgerald Kennedy was born in Brookline, Massachusetts, in May 1917, the second of nine children born into an ambitious, wealthy Irish-Catholic political dynasty. His father, Joseph P. Kennedy, was a ruthless Wall Street financier, movie mogul, and ambassador to Great Britain who instilled in his children an obsessive, relentless hunger for victory: 'We don't want any losers around here,' Joe Sr. constantly drilled into them. 'In this family, we want winners.' At their sprawling summer compound in Hyannis Port on Cape Cod, the Kennedy siblings played bruising, competitive games of touch football, sailed sleek Wianno Senior sloops across Nantucket Sound, and engaged in rapid-fire dinner table debates on international politics. Jack, however, was chronically frail and sickly from childhood, battling scarlet fever, severe digestive ailments, and excruciating spinal pain that required him to wear a heavy canvas back brace. Confined to bed for months at a time, the young boy devoured voluminous histories and biographies, developing a razor-sharp intellect, a photographic memory, and an effortless, self-deprecating wit that charmed everyone who crossed his path. Graduating from Harvard in 1940, his senior thesis on Britain's appeasement of Hitler became a best-selling book titled 'Why England Slept.' The intense family competition in Hyannis Port forged in Jack Kennedy an unquenchable drive to excel, masking his severe physical infirmities beneath a shield of effortless, sun-tanned charm and dazzling intellect. Young Jack learned early that wit and storytelling could bridge any social divide, giving him an instinctive gift for connecting with people from every walk of life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE MIDNIGHT SLICING OF PT-109
When the United States entered World War II, Kennedy was initially disqualified from military service due to his chronic, debilitating back problems. Refusing to sit out the war behind a desk, he used his father's political connections to obtain an active-duty naval commission, volunteering for hazardous combat duty commanding plywood Patrol Torpedo boats in the South Pacific. In the pitch-black, moonless midnight of August 2, 1943, twenty-six-year-old Lieutenant Kennedy was patrolling Blackett Strait in the Solomon Islands aboard PT-109. Suddenly, out of the ink-black darkness, the colossal two-thousand-ton Japanese destroyer Amagiri bore down on them at forty knots. Before Kennedy could wheel his engines to fire torpedoes, the steel bow of the destroyer sheared through PT-109 like a giant razor blade, slicing the wooden boat in half in a blinding fireball of aviation fuel. Two crewmen, Andrew Jackson Kirksey and Harold William Johnston, were vaporized instantly. The remaining eleven men were hurled into the burning, fuel-slicked sea, gasping for air amidst floating wreckage. As the destroyer disappeared into the night, Kennedy rounded up the survivors, swimming through flames to drag injured crewmen back to the floating, waterlogged forward hulk of the boat. The catastrophic collision in Blackett Strait proved in a single blinding instant that no amount of wealth or family privilege could shield a man from the brutal, unforgiving realities of modern warfare. The catastrophic explosion in the night tested the young commander's courage under fire, forcing him to make instantaneous life-and-death choices for his men.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SWIM TO PLUM PUDDING ISLAND
By daylight on August 2, it was obvious that the remains of PT-109 were slowly sinking. Enemy Japanese barges and aircraft patrolled the surrounding channels; surrender was unthinkable, as the Japanese rarely took prisoners alive in the Solomons. Pointing toward a tiny, uninhabited strip of sand and coral three miles to the southeast named Plum Pudding Island, Kennedy gave the order to abandon ship. One crewman, motor machinist Patrick McMahon, was horribly burned across his face, hands, and chest, completely unable to swim. Kennedy did not hesitate. Taking the long strap of McMahon's kapok life jacket between his teeth, Kennedy plunged into the ocean, swimming breaststroke for four agonizing hours while towing the burned sailor through the water. Exhausted, dehydrated, and suffering from severe spinal pain, Kennedy dragged McMahon onto the sandy shore of the tiny atoll, collapsing unconscious in the coral brush. For two days, the eleven men hid under palm fronds without fresh water, subsisting on bird droppings and bitter snail shells, watching Japanese patrol boats cruise past their tiny island. Kennedy's heroic endurance in the water, dragging a crippled comrade across open ocean while suffering agonizing spinal spasms, revealed the unshakeable inner steel that lay beneath his youthful demeanor. Clenching that strap between his teeth through hours of saltwater agony, Kennedy proved that moral responsibility to one's comrades transcends physical pain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE INSCRIPTION ON THE COCONUT SHELL
Desperate to find fresh water and contact Allied forces, Kennedy led his men on another grueling swim to Olasana Island, where they found ripe coconuts and rainwater trapped in leaves. While scouting neighboring Naru Island alone, Kennedy suddenly encountered two Melanesian islanders, Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana, who were operating as native coastwatchers behind Japanese lines for Australian intelligence. The islanders were initially terrified, fearing Kennedy was Japanese, but Jack established his identity by showing his naval dog tags. Lacking pen or paper to write a message, Kennedy plucked a green coconut from a nearby palm tree. Using his jackknife, he carved an urgent, cryptic message into the smooth green husk: 'NAURO ISL... COMMANDER... NATIVE KNOWS POS'IT... HE CAN PILOT... 11 ALIVE NEED SMALL BOAT... KENNEDY.' Handing the coconut to Gasa and Kumana, Kennedy instructed them to paddle their dugout canoe thirty-five miles through Japanese-controlled waters to the Allied base at Rendova. Risking their lives under the noses of Japanese patrols, the two islanders completed the perilous voyage and delivered the coconut to Australian coastwatcher Reginald Evans. The daring voyage of Biuku Gasa and Eroni Kumana through enemy patrol lines stood as a shining example of indigenous Melanesian courage in the Allied crusade against imperial Japanese aggression. The bravery of the island coastwatchers highlighted the indispensable contribution of local Pacific peoples in turning the tide against imperial conquest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE PAPERWEIGHT IN THE OVAL OFFICE
On the night of August 7, 1943, PT-157 rendezvoused with Kennedy and rescued all eleven surviving crewmen from Olasana Island. For his extraordinary heroism, Lieutenant Kennedy was awarded the Navy and Marine Corps Medal and the Purple Heart. When he returned home to Boston, the heroic saga of PT-109 was serialized in Reader's Digest by celebrated journalist John Hersey, launching Jack Kennedy onto the national stage as a genuine American war hero. Later in life, when asked by a young schoolboy how he had become a war hero, Kennedy smiled with his characteristic self-deprecating wit and replied: 'It was involuntary. They sank my boat.' But he never forgot the Melanesian scouts who had saved his life. Kennedy retrieved that carved coconut shell, had it encased in a block of clear protective plastic, and kept it on his desk in the Oval Office throughout his presidency as a permanent paperweight—a humble reminder that human courage and mutual trust can triumph over the darkest perils of war. That plastic-encased coconut paperweight sat silently upon the Resolute Desk throughout the Cuban Missile Crisis, a constant reminder of the terrible fragility of human life in the crucible of conflict. That simple coconut was more than a war trophy; it was a sacred talisman representing human solidarity, courage, and the gift of life against impossible odds.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE GOLDEN BACHELOR AND PROFILES IN COURAGE
In 1946, running in a working-class Boston congressional district, twenty-nine-year-old Jack Kennedy won his first election, knocking on tenement doors and charming Italian, Irish, and Polish immigrants. In 1952, he toppled Republican Brahmin Senator Henry Cabot Lodge Jr. in a sensational Senate victory. In Washington, Kennedy was the capital's most eligible and glamorous bachelor. In 1953, he married Jacqueline Lee Bouvier—a brilliant, aristocratic, French-speaking photojournalist whose elegance and poise would captivate the globe. While recovering from delicate and dangerous spinal fusion surgery in 1954, during which he was administered the Catholic last rites, Kennedy wrote 'Profiles in Courage,' a stirring study of eight historic United States senators who had bravely sacrificed their political careers to uphold constitutional principles over party loyalty. The book won the 1957 Pulitzer Prize for biography, cementing Kennedy's reputation as a rare combination of charismatic politician and serious intellectual statesman, perfectly positioning him for a run at the presidency in 1960. In 'Profiles in Courage,' Kennedy articulated the timeless truth that democratic statesmanship demands the willingness to defy popular passion in the service of enduring constitutional principles. The Pulitzer Prize recognized Kennedy's unique ability to examine political history through the lens of human character, courage, and moral decision-making.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE 1960 DEBATES AND THE NEW FRONTIER
In 1960, forty-three-year-old John F. Kennedy challenged Vice President Richard Nixon for the presidency. The defining moment of the campaign arrived on September 26, 1960, in a television studio in Chicago: the first televised presidential debate in world history. Seventy million Americans tuned in on black-and-white screens. Nixon, recovering from a painful knee infection and a bout of the flu, refused television makeup, wore an ill-fitting gray suit that blended into the backdrop, and visibly sweated under the hot studio lights. Kennedy, by contrast, was radiant, tanned from campaigning in California, wore a crisp dark suit, rested comfortably in his chair, and spoke with calm, confident authority directly into the camera lens. Radio listeners generally thought Nixon had won the debate on points; but television viewers overwhelmingly declared Kennedy the winner. Image and visual charisma had arrived in American politics. On November 8, 1960, Kennedy defeated Nixon in one of the closest popular vote elections in history, winning by just one hundred and twelve thousand votes out of sixty-eight million cast. The young boy from Hyannis Port had reached the summit of power, summoning a hopeful nation to cross the 'New Frontier.' The 1960 debates fundamentally transformed American democracy into a visual medium, where poise, telegenic charisma, and televised demeanor became just as influential as traditional political oratory. That historic televised debate marked the permanent arrival of modern electronic media as the supreme arbiter of American presidential politics.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
John F. Kennedy's triumph in 1960 inaugurated an era of youthful optimism, cultural glamour, and bold national ambition known as Camelot. But the presidency brought immediate, harrowing crises that pushed the world to the precipice of nuclear annihilation. Next week, we conclude our John F. Kennedy saga: the inaugural pledge to 'Ask not what your country can do for you,' his legendary White House wit, the bold promise to land on the moon, the thirteen terrifying days of the Cuban Missile Crisis, and the tragic loss in Dallas that shattered a nation's heart. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
